items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: you did work with him on occasion in recording situations, and I believe you said you did have an opportunity to talk to him and have a conversation with him.

ctx.x: Yeah. Well, actually, I think when we come to the forties and the Charlie Parker era and all that, we’ll read the quote and maybe discuss it then, actually, because it does pertain to the influence of Charlie Parker on soloists and on you in particular, or lack of influence, whatever. So I’d like to deal with that . . .
Well, the influence of Charlie Parker has been just unprecedented, really.
But I guess not enough, according to Lee. [laughs]

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWEE] Well, I think Parker would certainly, undoubtedly be the outstanding example... [INTERVIEWEE] I don't think anybody did much of that, did they, before Charlie Parker, I mean, you know?

ctx.x: But perhaps this being, as far as I know, the only really large scale study of at least a single jazz figure's technique of improvisation, suggests something about the mechanics of what improvising is.

Well, I think Parker would certainly, undoubtedly be the outstanding example, but I think this applies to almost any improvisation that I think you would hear coming out of a musician's instrument, and you would find this pattern

persisting, something that he would do according to the chord structure. You know, there'd be a figure or a number of different figures that he would use at a particular chord change, depending, you know, on the tempo and ...
